---
title: "F1 Score"
description: "The harmonic mean of precision and recall for a classification model."
term: "F1 Score"
letter: "F"
category: "Model Evaluation"
difficulty: "Beginner"

## Simple explanation

The F1 score combines precision and recall into one number. It is useful
when both false positives and false negatives matter, especially when
classes are imbalanced.

## Technical explanation

For positive-class precision $P$ and recall $R$, the F1 score is
$F_1 = 2\frac{PR}{P+R}$. Equivalently, using true positives (TP), false
positives (FP), and false negatives (FN):

$$
F_1 = \frac{2TP}{2TP+FP+FN}
$$

The score ranges from 0 to 1 when defined. Macro, micro, and weighted
averaging produce different summaries for multiclass settings.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Accuracy can obscure poor positive-class detection when classes are
imbalanced. F1 provides a single summary that penalizes low precision or
low recall, but it does not encode every application's error costs.

## How it works

Compute precision as $TP/(TP+FP)$ and recall as $TP/(TP+FN)$, then take
their harmonic mean. The harmonic mean is pulled down when either
component is low. The decision threshold affects TP, FP, and FN, and
therefore affects F1.

## Practical example

A classifier that flags potentially harmful content can be evaluated
with F1 when both missed harmful cases and incorrectly flagged benign
cases matter. The team should also inspect precision and recall
separately before choosing a threshold.

## Common misconceptions

- A high F1 score does not guarantee good performance for every subgroup
  or deployment setting.
- F1 ignores true negatives, so it may be unsuitable when that count is
  important.
- Two systems with the same F1 can have very different precision and
  recall.
